claim: The incidence of spinal cord injury (SCI) in the USA is around 18,000 new cases per year.
source: In the USA, the incidence of SCI is around 18,000 new cases per year, with a total prevalence ranging from 250,000 to 368,000 cases (National Spinal Cor Injury Statistical Center, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, 2021.

claim: The total prevalence of SCI in the USA ranges from 250,000 to 368,000 cases.
source: In the USA, the incidence of SCI is around 18,000 new cases per year, with a total prevalence ranging from 250,000 to 368,000 cases (National Spinal Cor Injury Statistical Center, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, 2021.

claim: The estimated lifetime cost per SCI patient is between $1.2 and $5.1 million.
source: The dramatic life event of SCI imposes a high socioeconomic burden, with an estimated lifetime cost between $1.2 and $5.1 million per patient (National Spinal Cor Injury Statistical Center, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, 2021.

claim: Lower post-surgery mean arterial pressure (MAP) predicts poor outcome in humans with SCI.
source: Prior retrospective observational single-center studies in humans suggest that lower post-surgery mean arterial pressure (MAP) predicts poor outcome (Cohn et al., 2010; Hawryluk et al., 2015; Saadeh et al., 2017; Ehsanian, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies (Cohn et al., 2010; Hawryluk et al., 2015; Saadeh et al., 2017; Ehsanian, 2020).

claim: Clinical guidelines focus on avoidance of hypotension by maintaining MAP >85 mmHg during the first 7 days of injury.
source: which have resulted in clinical guidelines focused on avoidance of hypotension by maintaining MAP >85 mmHg during the first 7 days of injury (Aarabi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aarabi et al., 2013.

claim: Decreased spinal cord perfusion leads to ischemia and additional tissue loss.
source: The rational for MAP augmentation to avoid hypotension is based on the hypothesis that decreased spinal cord prefusion leads to ischemia and additional tissue lost (Mautes et al., 2000; Soubeyrand et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mautes et al., 2000 and Soubeyrand et al., 2014.

claim: Experimentally raising MAP during acute SCI in animals by using vasopressors increases the risk for hemorrhage and consequent tissue damage.
source: Importantly, experimentally raising MAP during acute SCI in animals by using vasopressors increases the risk for hemorrhage and consequent tissue damage (Soubeyrand et al., 2014; Streijger et al., 2018; Guha et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Soubeyrand et al., 2014; Streijger et al., 2018; and Guha et al., 1987.

claim: In acute cervical patients with SCI, spinal cord hemorrhage correlates with poor prognosis for neurological recovery.
source: In acute cervical patients with SCI, spinal cord hemorrhage correlates with poor prognosis for neurological recovery (Miyanji et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Miyanji et al., 2007.

claim: Hypertension during SCI surgery (ultra-acute phase) predicts long-term functional recovery in rodent models.
source: Using the machine intelligence approach of topological data analysis, we have previously shown that hypertension during SCI surgery (ultra-acute phase) predicts long-term functional recovery in rodent models (Nielson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nielson et al., 2015.

claim: Operating room records from n = 94 patients (98 surgical records) from ZSFG and n = 33 patients (33 surgical records) from SCVMC were collected retrospectively.
source: Operating room (OR) records from n = 94 patients (98 surgical records, 3 patients with multiple surgeries) from the Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital (ZSFG, from 2005 to 2013) and n = 33 patients (33 surgical records) from the Santa Clara Valley Medical Center (SCVMC, from 2013 to 2015) that underwent spinal surgery were collected retrospectively.
evidence: The claim describes the data collection process and sample sizes from the two centers.

claim: For ZSFG, monitoring data was extracted from values manually recorded by the anesthesiologist at 5 min intervals (Q5).
source: For ZSFG, monitoring data was extracted from the values manually recorded by the anesthesiologist at 5 min intervals (Q5).
evidence: The claim describes the data collection methodology for ZSFG.

claim: For SCVMC, monitoring data was extracted from the Surgical Information Systems (SIS) at 1 min intervals (Q1).
source: For SCVMC, monitoring data was extracted from the Surgical Information Systems (SIS) (Alpharetta, GA) at 1 min intervals (Q1).
evidence: The claim describes the data collection methodology for SCVMC.

claim: The final cohort for exploratory topological data analysis included 118 patients with complete MAP and heart rate (HR) monitoring.
source: The final cohort for exploratory topological data analysis included 118 patients with complete MAP and heart rate (HR) monitoring.
evidence: The claim describes the final sample size for the analysis.

claim: For confirmatory regression analysis, 15 patients were excluded because AIS grade could not be extracted either at admission and/or discharge.
source: For confirmatory regression analysis, 15 patients were excluded because AIS grade could not be extracted either at admission and/or discharge (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes exclusion criteria for the regression analysis and references a figure.

claim: AIS improvement was defined as an increase of at least one AIS grade from admission to discharge.
source: AIS improvement was defined as an increase of at least one AIS grade from admission to discharge.
evidence: The claim defines the outcome measure used in the study.

claim: MAP values under 10 and above 200 mmHg as well as point-to-point changes greater than 40 mmHg were filtered as data artifacts.
source: Thus, MAP values under 10 and above 200 mmHg as well as point-to-point changes greater than 40 mmHg were filtered, as these instances were found to represent data artifacts.
evidence: The claim describes the data filtering criteria applied to the SCVMC data.

claim: The filtering process for SCVMC data was validated with an accuracy of 99.1%.
source: This process was validated by comparing clinical curated data and the extracted data from the script with an accuracy of 99.1%.
evidence: The claim reports the validation accuracy of the data filtering process.

claim: Isomap is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that uses multidimensional scaling (MDS) with geodesic distances instead of Euclidean distances.
source: Isomap is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that uses multidimensional scaling (MDS) with geodesic distances instead of the Euclidean distances as the classic MDS does, and it has been suggested before for health data (Weng et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim describes the Isomap algorithm and cites a prior application in health data.

claim: The minimal k that produced a connected NNG was k = 3.
source: For selecting k, we considered the minimal k the smallest one that produced a connected NNG, in our case k = 3.
evidence: The claim reports a parameter selection result from the analysis.

claim: A d = 4 (four dimensions kept in the k = 6 Isomap) was chosen as the final solution.
source: A d = 4 (four dimensions kept in the k = 6 Isomap) was chosen for being the one at the 'elbow' of the RV, the one that minimized WD0 in k = 6 Isomap and presented a good compromised WD1.
evidence: The claim describes the final parameter selection for the dimensionality reduction.

claim: The walktrap algorithm solution was 47 random steps, producing a dendrogram tree of connectivity which maximal modularity cut the tree in 11 clusters.
source: This solution was 47 random steps, producing a dendrogram tree of connectivity which maximal modularity cut the tree in 11 clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim reports the clustering results from the walktrap algorithm.

claim: Network analysis suggested that time outside of an optimum MAP range (hypotension or hypertension) during surgery was associated with lower likelihood of neurological recovery at hospital discharge.
source: Network analysis suggested that time outside of an optimum MAP range (hypotension or hypertension) during surgery was associated with lower likelihood of neurological recovery at hospital discharge.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the network analysis.

claim: Logistic and LASSO regression confirmed the network analysis findings, revealing an optimal MAP range of 76–[104-117] mmHg associated with neurological recovery.
source: Logistic and LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression confirmed these findings, revealing an optimal MAP range of 76–[104-117] mmHg associated with neurological recovery.
evidence: The claim summarizes the confirmatory regression analysis results.

claim: Clusters of patients showing an extreme variation of MAP were highly enriched with patients with no AIS recovery.
source: In contrast, clusters of patients showing an extreme variation of MAP were highly enriched with patients with no AIS recovery and patients with more severe AIS grades at discharge (AIS A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim describes an observation from the network analysis and references a figure.

claim: The quadratic model showed a significant improvement over the linear model with lower LOOCV error.
source: However, polynomial logistic regression demonstrated a significant quadratic fit (Table 2) with lower LOOCV error than the linear model, indicating that a quadratic form of aMAP better predicts the probability of improvement.
evidence: The claim reports the results of model comparison using LOOCV error.

claim: The cubic model did not show significant improvement over the quadratic one.
source: Notably, the cubic model did not show significant improvement over the quadratic one.
evidence: The claim reports the results of model comparison.

claim: The significance of the quadratic fit holds even after accounting for covariates (aHR, length of surgery, days from surgery to discharge, age, and AIS grade at admission).
source: The significance of the quadratic fit holds even after accounting for the covariates (Table 3, 4), and none of the terms in the covariates-only model had a significant coefficient (Table 5).
evidence: The claim reports the results of covariate-adjusted regression analysis.

claim: None of the terms in the covariates-only model had a significant coefficient.
source: The significance of the quadratic fit holds even after accounting for the covariates (Table 3, 4), and none of the terms in the covariates-only model had a significant coefficient (Table 5).
evidence: The claim reports the results of the covariates-only model.

claim: In the cervical cohort, the quadratic aMAP maintained significance.
source: Running the same full model with just the cervical patients resulted in similar results as compared to the full model on the entire cohort, maintaining the quadratic aMAP significance (Table 8).
evidence: The claim reports the results of subgroup analysis in cervical patients.

claim: In the non-cervical cohort, there was no significant association of the quadratic aMAP to recovery.
source: In the non-cervical cohort, we did not find a significant association of the quadratic aMAP to recovery (Table 9).
evidence: The claim reports the results of subgroup analysis in non-cervical patients.

claim: A MAP range from 76 to 104 mmHg was optimal in the dataset since it produced the most reproducible prediction of recovery (average LOOCV prediction accuracy of 61.16%).
source: Interestingly, the logistic LASSO regression with LOOCV revealed that a MAP range from 76 to 104 mmHg was optimal in our dataset since it produced the most reproducible prediction of recovery (average LOOCV prediction accuracy of 61.16%; Figure 4c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Table 9).
evidence: The claim reports the results of LASSO regression analysis for symmetric MAP range.

claim: The logistic LASSO found the range 76–117 mmHg to be the most predictive of recovery (average cross-validation prediction accuracy of 57.28%).
source: The association of the patient distribution in the network plateau at a range of 76–116 mmHg (Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the logistic LASSO found the range 76–117 mmHg be the most predictive of recovery (average cross-validation prediction accuracy of 57.28%; Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, Table 10).
evidence: The claim reports the results of LASSO regression analysis for asymmetric MAP range.

claim: The model predicting AIS improvement had a cross-validated AUC of 0.74.
source: The model predicting AIS improvement had a cross-validated AUC of 0.74, the model predicting AIS A at discharge had a cross-validated AUC of 0.88, and the model predicting AIS D at discharge had a cross-validation AUC of 0.84.
evidence: The claim reports the prediction performance of the AIS improvement model.

claim: The model predicting AIS A at discharge had a cross-validated AUC of 0.88.
source: The model predicting AIS improvement had a cross-validated AUC of 0.74, the model predicting AIS A at discharge had a cross-validated AUC of 0.88, and the model predicting AIS D at discharge had a cross-validation AUC of 0.84.
evidence: The claim reports the prediction performance of the AIS A at discharge model.

claim: The model predicting AIS D at discharge had a cross-validation AUC of 0.84.
source: The model predicting AIS improvement had a cross-validated AUC of 0.74, the model predicting AIS A at discharge had a cross-validated AUC of 0.88, and the model predicting AIS D at discharge had a cross-validation AUC of 0.84.
evidence: The claim reports the prediction performance of the AIS D at discharge model.

claim: Both the parsimonious model predicting AIS improvement and the one predicting AIS A at discharge included quadratic aMAP as an important predictor.
source: Both the parsimonious model predicting AIS improvement and the one predicting AIS A at discharge included quadratic aMAP as an important predictor.
evidence: The claim describes the features included in the best prediction models.

claim: The model predicting AIS D did not include any of the MAP associated terms.
source: The model predicting AIS D did not include any of the MAP associated terms, suggesting that patients discharged with AIS D can be predicted without considering their MAP during OR.
evidence: The claim describes the features included in the AIS D prediction model.

claim: Training the models predicting AIS improvement and AIS A at discharge without a MAP component reduced the model performance considerably (AUC, AIS improvement: 0.74 vs. 0.52; AIS A discharge: 0.88 vs. 0.78).
source: Training the models predicting AIS improvement and AIS A at discharge but without a MAP component (quadratic MAP term or time of MAP out of range) reduced the model performance considerably (AUC, AIS improvement: 0.74 vs. 0.52; AIS A discharge: 0.88 vs. 0.78).
evidence: The claim reports the results of ablation analysis showing the importance of MAP features.

claim: Recent analysis of high-frequency ICU monitoring data and systematic meta-analysis of post-surgery management suggest that the MAP threshold to avoid is actually lower (~75 mmHg) than the current recommendation of 85 mmHg.
source: Recent analysis of high-frequency ICU monitoring data (Hawryluk et al., 2015) and systematic meta-analysis of post-surgery management (Saadeh et al., 2017) suggest that the MAP threshold to avoid is actually lower (~75 mmHg) than the current recommendation of 85 mmHg, and that MAP management might be effective at shorter duration (< 5 days post-injury) than the 7-day goal (Saadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hawryluk et al., 2015 and Saadeh et al., 2017.

claim: MAP management might be effective at shorter duration (< 5 days post-injury) than the 7-day goal.
source: Recent analysis of high-frequency ICU monitoring data (Hawryluk et al., 2015) and systematic meta-analysis of post-surgery management (Saadeh et al., 2017) suggest that the MAP threshold to avoid is actually lower (~75 mmHg) than the current recommendation of 85 mmHg, and that MAP management might be effective at shorter duration (< 5 days post-injury) than the 7-day goal (Saadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saadeh et al., 2017.

claim: High blood pressure induced by vasopressors can translate to increased risk of hemorrhage in the injured spinal cord, exacerbating tissue damage.
source: The physiological rational is that high blood pressure induced by vasopressors can translate to increased risk of hemorrhage in the injured spinal cord, exacerbating tissue damage (Soubeyrand et al., 2014; Streijger et al., 2018; Guha et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Soubeyrand et al., 2014; Streijger et al., 2018; and Guha et al., 1987.

claim: The use of some vasopressors might cause more complications in patients.
source: Moreover, the use of some vasopressors might cause more complications in patients (Inoue et al., 2014) while also potentially contributing to intra-spinal hemorrhage.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Inoue et al., 2014.

claim: Dobutamine can correct for hemodynamic anomalies and increase blood flow to the spinal cord while reducing the risk of hemorrhage compared to norepinephrine.
source: Specifically, the authors demonstrated that dobutamine can correct for hemodynamic anomalies and increase blood flow to the spinal cord while reducing the risk of hemorrhage compared to norepinephrine.
evidence: The claim refers to findings from Williams et al., 2020 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Patients with cervical SCI present more frequently with hemodynamic and cardiac abnormalities than patients with thoracolumbar SCI.
source: Patients with cervical SCI present more frequently with hemodynamic and cardiac abnormalities than patients with thoracolumbar SCI, increasing the need for treatment (Lehmann et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lehmann et al., 1987.

claim: Sympathetic dysregulation in upper cord injuries reduces sympathetic tone likely causing reduced heart contractility, bradycardia, and hypotension.
source: This is due to sympathetic dysregulation in upper cord injuries, which reduces sympathetic tone likely causing reduced heart contractility, bradycardia, and hypotension (Lehmann et al., 1987; Myers et al., 2007; Teasell et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lehmann et al., 1987; Myers et al., 2007; and Teasell et al., 2000.

claim: Deviation from the optimal MAP range of 76–[104-117] mmHg during SCI surgery predicts lower probability of neurological recovery.
source: We show that deviation from this optimal MAP range during SCI surgery predicts lower probability of neurological recovery and suggest new targets for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The low boundary of 76 mmHg found in the ultra-early analysis supports previous suggestions for lowering the intervention threshold.
source: The low boundary of 76 mmHg found in our ultra-early analysis further supports previous suggestions for lowering the intervention threshold (Cohn et al., 2010; Hawryluk et al., 2015; Saadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings and citations to prior work.

claim: There is an upper boundary to MAP management between 104 and 117 mmHg, above which the probability of improvement is reduced.
source: On the other side, we find an upper boundary to MAP management between 104 and 117 mmHg, above which the probability of improvement is reduced.
evidence: The claim is based on the study's data analysis results.

claim: Normotensive MAP during surgery predicts AIS improvement in patients with cervical SCI but not in patients with lower injuries.
source: We observed that normotensive MAP during surgery predicts AIS improvement in patients with cervical SCI but not in patients with lower injuries (thoracic, lumbar, and sacral).
evidence: The claim is based on the study's subgroup analysis results.

claim: Topology-based analytics can uncover associations for hypothesis generation during exploratory analysis in a cross-species validation.
source: First, we demonstrate that topology-based analytics can undercover associations for hypothesis generation during exploratory analysis in a cross-species validation.
evidence: The claim is based on the successful application of the method in this study and prior animal studies.

claim: Patient similarity networks are useful and interpretable representations of multidimensional datasets that capture associations during exploratory analysis.
source: Second, we provide further illustration that patient similarity networks are useful and interpretable representations of multidimensional datasets that capture associations during exploratory analysis that can then be validated by network-independent confirmatory analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on the successful application of the method in this study.

claim: Isomap combined with topology-based metrics can successfully evaluate embedding solutions.
source: Third, we successfully combine Isomap, a non-linear dimensionality reduction method, with topology-based metrics to evaluate embedding solutions.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodological approach used in this study.

claim: The workflow captures representations of multidimensional time-series of different lengths into a network that is actionable.
source: Lastly, our workflow captures representations of multidimensional time-series of different lengths into a network that is actionable.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodological approach used in this study.

claim: The study has limitations including the retrospective nature of the analysis, the relatively small sample size, and the use of an estimated ordinal scale (AIS grade) as an indicator of neurological recovery.
source: Limitations of this study include the retrospective nature of the analysis, the relatively small sample size (although large for SCI), and the use of an estimated ordinal scale (AIS grade) as an indicator of neurological recovery.
evidence: The claim explicitly states the limitations of the study.

claim: Other factors not considered in this analysis such as MAP levels before or after surgery or the use of vasopressors might influence the results.
source: An important consideration is the difficulty of determining AIS grade early after injury. Moreover, other factors not considered in this analysis such as MAP levels before or after surgery or the use of vasopressors might influence the results.
evidence: The claim acknowledges potential confounding factors not included in the analysis.

claim: Clustering the network of patients through a random-walk algorithm, Walktrap, revealed 11 different clusters where patients were regarded to share intra-operative hemodynamic phenotypes.
source: Clustering the network of patients through a random-walk algorithm, Walktrap (Pons and Latapy, 2005), revealed 11 different clusters where patients were regarded to share intra-operative hemodynamic phenotypes (Figure 2 andFigure 2—figure supplement 1f-h).
evidence: The claim reports the clustering results from the network analysis.

claim: The workflow was unsupervised: only the OR hemodynamic time-series was used to derive patient clustering.
source: Importantly, this workflow was unsupervised: only the OR hemodynamic time-series was used to derive patient clustering, and therefore any association captured by the network must be dependent on hemodynamic patterns.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach of the network analysis.

claim: Patients with recovery localized to clusters associated with a middle range of MAP.
source: Mapping the proportion of patients with AIS improvement onto the similarity network (Figure 2h–j) revealed that patients with recovery localized to clusters associated with a middle range of MAP (Figure 2k).
evidence: The claim describes an observation from the network analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Clusters with higher proportion of patients with recovery had an aMAP in a middle range, while clusters with higher proportion of patients without recovery presented extreme aMAPs.
source: Clusters of higher proportion of patients with recovery had an aMAP in a middle range, while clusters with higher proportion of patients without recovery presented extreme aMAPs (k).
evidence: The claim describes an observation from Figure 2k.

claim: The linear model showed a significant improvement over the null model with a positive association, suggesting that the higher the aMAP, the higher the probability of AIS grade improvement.
source: The linear model showed a significant improvement over the null model with a positive association, suggesting that the higher the aMAP, the higher the probability of AIS grade improvement.
evidence: The claim reports the results of the linear logistic regression model.

claim: A spline model of degree 2 resulted in a significant fit over the linear model.
source: A spline model of degree 2 resulted in a significant fit over the linear model (Table 2) while a spline model of degree 3 resulted in a similar fit as compared to the cubic model.
evidence: The claim reports the results of the spline model comparison.

claim: There was no evidence from which to choose between the spline model of degree 2 and the quadratic model.
source: There was no evidence from which to choose between the spline model of degree 2 and the quadratic model.
evidence: The claim reports the results of model comparison.

claim: In the AIS A at admission cohort, the linear aMAP coefficient was significant and the quadratic term was close to significant (p = 0.14).
source: The resulting model showed the linear aMAP coefficient to be significant and the quadratic term close to significant (p = 0.14) with the second biggest coefficient (Table 6).
evidence: The claim reports the results of the subgroup analysis in AIS A patients.

claim: A likelihood ratio test between a linear model with covariates and a quadratic model with covariates resulted in p-values = 0.07 for the AIS A cohort.
source: A likelihood ratio test between a linear model with covariates and a quadratic model with covariates resulted in p-values = 0.07.
evidence: The claim reports the results of the likelihood ratio test for the AIS A cohort.

claim: In the full model with covariates fitted to the entire cohort, none of the AIS grades at admission had significant coefficients.
source: On the other hand, in the full model with covariates fitted to the entire cohort, none of the AIS grades at admission had significant coefficients, which suggested that the non-linear relationship of MAP with neurological recovery was sustained across injury severity in that model.
evidence: The claim reports the results of the full covariate model.

claim: Days to discharge does not associate with probability of improvement (p = 0.32).
source: We first fitted a logistic regression model with AIS improvement as response and days to discharge as the only predictor. This resulted in a non-significant p-value of p = 0.32, suggesting that days to discharge does not associate with probability of improvement.
evidence: The claim reports the results of logistic regression analysis.

claim: A linear model with days to discharge as a response and quadratic aMAP as predictors resulted in a significant coefficient of the quadratic term (p = 0.047).
source: Second, we fitted a linear model with days to discharge as a response and quadratic aMAP (both linear and quadratic terms) as predictors. This resulted as a significant coefficient of the quadratic term (p = 0.047), although the model was not significant (p = 0.13 for the F statistic) and the adjusted R2 was small (0.0217).
evidence: The claim reports the results of linear regression analysis.

claim: Days to discharge and MAP do not interact to predict AIS improvement (interaction days to discharge with aMAP: linear term p = 0.61; quadratic term p = 0.91).
source: We also investigated whether days to discharge interacts with MAP and quadratic MAP to predict AIS improvement, with no significant results on the interaction (interaction days to discharge with aMAP: linear term p = 0.61; quadratic term p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim reports the results of interaction analysis.

claim: Eliminating days to discharge from the full covariate model predicting AIS improvement does not have a major effect on the model fit.
source: Finally, eliminating days to discharge from the full covariate model predicting AIS improvement does not have a major effect on the model fit. A likelihood ratio test between both models shows a non-significant change in variance explained (p = 0.729) with a deviance difference of ~0.1%.
evidence: The claim reports the results of model comparison.

claim: The non-linear relationship between aMAP and AIS improvement is independent of the days from surgery to discharge.
source: All together indicates that the non-linear relationship between aMAP and AIS improvement is independent of the days from surgery to discharge.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the series of analyses examining the relationship between days to discharge and MAP.

claim: The association of the patient distribution in the network was most highly associated with the range 73–107 mmHg for the symmetric range.
source: Calculating the assortativity coefficient (Ar) of the network for each range revealed that the distribution of patients in the network was most highly associated with the range 73–107 mmHg for the symmetric range (b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim reports the results of exploratory network analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The association of the patient distribution in the network plateau at a range of 76–116 mmHg for the asymmetric range study.
source: The association of the patient distribution in the network plateau at a range of 76–116 mmHg (Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim reports the results of exploratory network analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The upper limit of the MAP range is probably anywhere between 104 and 117 mmHg.
source: Therefore, from a modeling perspective, we broadly conclude that the upper limit of the MAP range is probably anywhere between 104 and 117 mmHg.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the comparison of the two LASSO models.

claim: Training the same model for AIS D but with the inclusion of the quadratic aMAP term resulted in slightly worse prediction performance (AUC 0.84 vs. 0.83).
source: In fact, training the same model but with the inclusion of the quadratic aMAP term resulted in slightly worse prediction performance (AUC 0.84 vs. 0.83).
evidence: The claim reports the results of model comparison for AIS D prediction.

claim: Level 4 evidence from a small single-center case series study in the 1990s suggested that MAP augmentation to 85–90 mmHg during the first 5–7 days after injury was linked to neurological recovery in acute SCI.
source: Level 4 evidence from a small single-center case series study in the 1990s suggested that MAP augmentation to 85–90 mmHg during the first 5–7 days after injury was linked to neurological recovery in acute SCI (Levi et al., 1993; Vale et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Levi et al., 1993 and Vale et al., 1997.

claim: The results from the 1990s studies are the basis of clinical guidelines for avoidance of hypotension in acute SCI management.
source: These results are the basis of clinical guidelines for avoidance of hypotension in acute SCI management (Aarabi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aarabi et al., 2013.

claim: The arbitrary, recommended MAP goal has been controversial.
source: However, while numerous clinical studies support MAP augmentation, the arbitrary, recommended MAP goal has been controversial (Cohn et al., 2010; Hawryluk et al., 2015; Saadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The present study represents a multicenter, data-driven, and cross-validated re-evaluation in a different setting (during surgery as compared with prior ICU studies).
source: The present study represents a multicenter, data-driven, and cross-validated re-evaluation in a different setting (during surgery as compared with prior ICU studies).
evidence: The claim describes the nature and contribution of the present study.

claim: The analysis supports that there must be a MAP range during surgery at which neurological recovery is maximized.
source: Our analysis support that there must be a MAP range during surgery at which neurological recovery is maximized, providing further evidence that MAP management for maintaining normotension might be more beneficial for patient outcome than MAP augmentation for hypotension avoidance alone (Ehsanian, 2020; Nielson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Recent results in acute experimental SCI suggest controlling for hemodynamic dysregulation through a cardiac-focused treatment instead of using standard vasopressors such as norepinephrine.
source: In fact, recent results in acute experimental SCI suggest controlling for hemodynamic dysregulation through a cardiac-focused treatment instead of using standard vasopressors such as norepinephrine (Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2020.

claim: The findings together with previous work translate animal study results to humans, indicating that prolonged periods of hypertension early after injury can be a predictor of poor neurological recovery in patients with SCI.
source: Our findings together with previous work (Ehsanian, 2020) also translate these animal study results to humans, indicating that prolonged periods of hypertension early after injury can be a predictor of poor neurological recovery in patients with SCI.
evidence: The claim is based on the study's findings and supported by a citation.

claim: Hemodynamic instability early after injury could serve as a prognostic physiology-based biomarker in a subset of the population.
source: Hemodynamic instability early after injury could serve as a prognostic physiology-based biomarker in a subset of the population, providing a potential tool for precision medicine in SCI.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: The work constitutes a successful story of translating machine intelligence analytical tools from animals to humans.
source: Hence, our work constitutes a successful story of translating machine intelligence analytical tools from animals to humans.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the successful application of methods from prior animal studies to human data.
